newsitem.title: GERMANY: German soldiers toil to hold back swollen Oder.
newsitem.headline: German soldiers toil to hold back swollen Oder.

text.p: Thousands of German soldiers fought tirelessly on Thursday to save a damaged dike on the River Oder from bursting open and unleashing a potentially catastrophic flood.

Military personnel, aid workers and villagers worked steadily to patch up a section of a dike near Hohenwutzen, after foundations cracked under the weight of two weeks of floods and threatened to burst completely.
"The chances of beating the sheer force of nature in this area are no higher than 10 to 15 percent," Brandenburg interior minister Alwin Ziel said of the situation in Hohenwutzen.
"The situation is not getting better, but rather more critical day by day," he said.

But state environment minister Matthias Platzek said it was amazing the dike had held at all. "It is a definitely a small wonder that a break in the Hohenwutzen dike has been avoided up to now," Platzek told German ARD television.

Some of the worst floods this century have hit neighbouring Poland and the Czech Republic this month, claiming more than 100 lives. No deaths have been reported in Germany but homes, businesses and farms have been extensively damaged.

Four people have died after a week of flooding and heavy rain throughout Romania and tens of thousands remain homeless in Poland as Germany, Poland and the European Commission begin exploring ways to provide relief for the flood victims.
Helicopters were dumping five-ton sacks of sand at the foot of the dike near Hohenwutzen to reinforce two areas where its foundations had cracked under the weight of the water.
Should the dike break, local officials said a wall of water several metres high would rush into the fertile Oder valley.

Nearly two dozen villages would initially be engulfed and, if a second line of dikes failed, the tide could flow through the rest of the valley filling a basin that covers 800 square km and contains over 70 villages and towns.

Around 10,000 residents of the Oder valley region on Germany's border with Poland were evacuated late on Wednesday, after the dike at Hohenwutzen threatened to give way. About 5,000 people were evacuated from the region last week.

While soldiers were piling trees, gravel and sandbags to secure the inland side of the dam that had sheared off under the weight of the flood, divers from a volunteer water rescue group worked to secure a 100 metre-long sheet of plastic on the dike near Hohenwutzen six metres underwater.

"We hope we can put up a barrier on the most threatened spots to keep the water from seeping through the dike," said Thomas Reim, 31, of Bremerhaven. "It's a little dangerous because you can't see a thing and the current is very strong."

Once the bread basket of communist East Germany, the area was drained 250 years ago by King Frederick the Great of Prussia to create fertile farmland out of the Oderbruch, which means the "Oder swamp", changing the course of the river.

The last time the dike broke was in 1947, near Reitwein, at the southern end of the Oderbruch. This time the weakest point is near Hohenwutzen, where in a sharp westward bend the water has been pressing relentlessly against the dikes for two weeks.
The dikes have already broken further south, submerging over 100 homes, and new weak spots have been appearing daily.

Steady flood levels and heavy rains made matters worse, where 5,000 soldiers were toiling to patch the dike and prevent a total break. Soldiers had to be removed from the dike periodically whenever the danger of it bursting became acute.

The picturesque riverside village Hohenwutzen has been transformed into the focal point of Germany's largest peacetime military operation. Soldiers lay sleeping on the muddy banks, or can be seen eating lentil soup from dirty green mess kits while military vehicles roar up and down the main road.

"We've been on our feet for 36 hours, some even for 49 hours," said navy seaman Holk Schilling, who was on the dike when it collapsed. "I could feel my heart drop into my stomach when the ground slipped out from under my feet."
Army captain Michael Schierenberg fixed his red beret and looked out over the swollen river. "It would be a miracle if the dike held -- but why shouldn't miracles happen?"
